Hybrid: NPU prefill, HRX decode (--device hybrid)#

1bit serve -m Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_K_M.gguf --device hybrid --prefill-provider <program>

Hybrid serves a .gguf with the prompt processed on one device and the tokens generated on another: a prefill provider computes the prompt's KV cache, and the HRX llama-server (docs/hrx.md) decodes from it on HRX0. The provider is the engine's NPU route; the public tree knows it only as a program with the contract below, the way -DONEBIT_NPU_PRIVATE keeps the NPU kernels out of the repository (docs/npu.md). Without a provider, --device hybrid is --device hrx with one slot.

In a build without HRX the decoder is the same llama-server on the CPU, so the route runs (and is tested) on any machine.

What happens per request#

  1. Template and tokenize on the backend. For /v1/chat/completions serve asks the llama-server child for the templated prompt (/apply-template) and its ids (/tokenize, add_special and parse_special on, as the server itself tokenizes); /v1/completions tokenizes its prompt string. The provider sees exactly the ids the backend would have prefilled.
  2. The provider prefills. serve writes the ids to a file in the backend's slot directory and runs the provider. It writes a llama.cpp sequence-state file for the prompt.
  3. Restore into slot 0. POST /slots/0?action=restore loads the file into the one slot; serve checks the slot holds all the prompt's tokens.
  4. Decode. The request is forwarded with id_slot 0 and cache_prompt true. llama-server finds the prompt in the slot, re-evaluates its last token (it always does, for the logits), and generates. The reply, streamed or not, is relayed as for every device.

One line per request on stderr: hybrid: N prompt tokens: prefill X ms, restore Y ms, first byte Z ms (the provider's own prefill_ms when it reports one, else its wall time; the restore from the backend's timing; first byte measured in serve from the start of the handoff).

Fallback. Any failure on the way (no text prompt, a provider that exits non-zero, times out or writes no file, a restore that fails or holds fewer tokens) is said on stderr with its reason, and the request is forwarded as it came: the backend prefills it itself. Without a provider named, serve says so once at start. The device is never unusable because the provider is.

One slot. Hybrid runs the backend with -np 1 and --slot-save-path, and serializes handoffs: a request holds the slot from its handoff until the backend has started on it (its first byte), after which llama-server itself defers the next restore until the slot is free. --parallel > 1 is refused; so are --mtp, --dflash, --mmproj, --moe-slots, a role (--embedding, --reranking) and --pm, and the GGUF's own MTP head is not used: nothing but the prompt's KV is handed over, and a drafter would draft over a cache it did not compute.

The provider contract#

<provider> --tokens <ids file> --out <state file> --model <model path> [--elfs <dir>]
--tokens the prompt's token ids, one decimal id per line, in order
--out where to write the state: a bare filename inside the backend's --slot-save-path directory (serve chooses it; the backend restores by that name)
--model the model file serve was given (-m)
--elfs passed when ONEBIT_HYBRID_ELFS is set: where the provider's kernels are
stdout one JSON line, last: {"n_tokens": N, "argmax": id, "prefill_ms": x}; n_tokens must equal the ids given (checked), argmax is the next-token argmax after the prompt (for diagnostics), prefill_ms is optional
exit 0 on success; anything else, or no file, is the fallback above
environment ONEBIT_HYBRID_BACKEND_URL=http://127.0.0.1:<port>, the decoding llama-server's address (a test provider makes its file through it; a real one has no use for it), plus serve's own environment
time limit ONEBIT_HYBRID_PREFILL_TIMEOUT_S (default 600): SIGTERM, then SIGKILL

The state file is what llama_state_seq_save_file writes and /slots/<id>?action=restore reads (llama.cpp src/llama-context.cpp, src/llama-kv-cache.cpp state_write_meta / state_write_data): the file magic and version, the token count and ids, then the KV cells of sequence 0 at positions 0..N-1: cell count, each cell's position and sequence ids, then per layer the K type, row size and N rows, then V the same way (transposed or not, as the server's cache is: v_trans 0 with flash attention, which HRX uses). The K rows are post-RoPE keys, as llama.cpp stores them; the cache type is the backend's (f16 by default), so a provider computing in another type converts. A provider must match the version of the pinned llama.cpp (third_party/llama.cpp): the restore refuses another.

Naming: --prefill-provider PATH or ONEBIT_HYBRID_PREFILL=PATH; ONEBIT_HYBRID_ELFS=DIR adds --elfs DIR.

Tests#

  • tests/hybrid_route.sh (CTest hybrid_route, no model, no NPU): tests/fake_backend.py stands in for llama-server and tests/fake_prefill_provider.py (FAKE_PREFILL_COPY=1) for the NPU engine. Checks what reaches the backend (id_slot 0, cache_prompt on, the slot directory), the stderr lines, the fallbacks (no provider; a provider that fails), the refused flags and --print-backend.
  • tests/hybrid_e2e.sh (CTest hybrid_e2e with ONEBIT_SERVE_TEST_GGUF; skips without a model or a llama-server): a real model through the whole path. The fake provider makes a real state file by having the decoding llama-server itself prefill the ids into slot 0 and save the slot, so the handoff is exercised end to end with no NPU. Checked: the greedy reply equals the plain --device cpu reply, and the backend's prompt_n is 1 (the re-evaluated last token), not the prompt length.

Status#

The plumbing (this document) is public. The NPU prefill provider, its kernels and its state-file writer are the engine's private NPU work; what it measures on Strix Halo is reported there when it lands.

What this pin can measure, measured (strixhalo, 2026-10-30, engine 38e29a2 + the #612 branch's lock commit, HRX llama-server 40c4ccb76, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-Q4_K_M, ctx 8192, a 307-token prompt and 8 greedy tokens, 3 requests each, under ~/.local/bin/gpu-hold -l "pi i612"):

route wall for the request the route's own breakdown
--device hrx --parallel 1 101 / 102 ms, after one 559 ms warm-up the backend prefills the prompt itself
--device hybrid + tests/fake_prefill_provider.py 356 / 370 / 390 ms prefill 212-239 ms, restore 6-7 ms, first byte 351-385 ms

The number that outlives the fake provider is the restore: 6-7 ms for 307 tokens. That is all the handoff itself costs (POST /slots/0?action=restore), so a hybrid can only win if the provider beats the backend's own prefill of the prompt by more than that -- and the backend prefills these 307 tokens inside those ~95 ms. With the fake provider it cannot: that provider prefills by asking the same llama-server, so the request pays for the prompt twice (212-239 ms) and the row above is a loss by construction, which is exactly what it shows.

What this pin cannot measure, and why. No real NPU prefill provider exists in this tree or in this build: it is the private NPU work (docs/npu.md, "Add-on routes"), and it needs the NPU device. The NPU prefill numbers this repository does have are four orders of magnitude from the gate above -- 58.14 s for a 5-token batched chunk on the 27B (docs/npu-leaderboard.md, record 27b-prefill-batched-20261027, engine 800cf6f era, add-on npu-dx 1e89468d4). So on this box the hybrid row is a measured loss, not a route waiting for a benchmark: at 58 s per chunk the handoff adds minutes where the backend needs 95 ms. It stays marked "not at this pin" in engine#612 until a real provider lands; quote that provider's own prefill figure when it does.

Running beside the GPU#

Hybrid is the one route that needs the NPU and the iGPU at the same time: the provider prefills on the NPU while the llama-server decodes on HRX0. That used to be blocked by fleet policy -- every NPU run was serialised behind the GPU queue -- on the strength of a third-party report (halogen-flash-server 0.16, 2026-10-02, never reproduced here) that concurrent GPU+NPU work could hang the box or corrupt NPU results while the GPU fabric clock (FCLK) changed level. It was measured on strixhalo and it does not reproduce. The fleet no longer serialises NPU work behind the GPU: an NPU run takes the NPU device lock (/tmp/1bit-npu-device.lock) and nothing else, and arena scoring carries a "GPU busy" column instead of demanding an idle box.

What was run: 40 reps of the arena GU oracle (~/wt/npu-arena/oracle.sh GU, the b8 pre-blocked-B leader rebuilt from source each time, byte-exact int32 on seeds 1-3 plus a median of 5 launches) in four cells -- GPU idle or busy, FCLK auto or held at the top level (manual + top pp_dpm_fclk) -- 5 reps per cell in two independent passes. The GPU load was HRX llama-bench on Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M, pp512/tg128 looping (34-52 bench rows per busy cell, so it ran throughout), started 20 s before the NPU reps. FCLK level, Tctl and GPU busy% were sampled at 1 Hz through every cell.

GPU FCLK ms/launch, median of 5 (two passes) GB/s (two passes) byte-exact resets/MODE2
idle auto 10.52 / 10.79 8.47 / 8.26 10/10 PASS 0
idle held 10.76 / 10.92 8.29 / 8.16 10/10 PASS 0
busy auto 12.04 / 12.04 7.40 / 7.40 10/10 PASS 0
busy held 10.85 / 12.01 8.22 / 7.42 10/10 PASS 0
  • 160 byte-exact checks, all PASS, and zero amdgpu GPU reset / MODE2 / ring-timeout lines in journalctl -k in any cell of either pass. The fabric clock demonstrably changed level during NPU runs in the auto cells (18 one-second samples at level 7 against 50 at level 6 in one busy cell).
  • Kernel 7.3.0-rc4-1bit-perfopt+, SMU firmware 0x0a640700 (100.7.0), DMUB 0x09003F00, device 0x1586 (Radeon 8060S), BIOS 1.09 (2026-05-08). That is the hardware/firmware pair this verdict is for; a vendor report about other firmware is neither confirmed nor denied by it.
  • The number to plan hybrid around is the busy-GPU stream cost: a GPU-busy NPU stream keeps ~87 % of its bandwidth, 7.40 GB/s against 8.2-8.5 idle (per launch 10.5-10.9 ms -> 12.0 ms), and it is 7.40 to two decimals in both passes. Budget the provider at ~13 % below its solo figure while the decoder is working.
  • FCLK does not buy that back, and an earlier claim of ours that it did is retracted. One pass had the hold removing the penalty (10.85 ms held against 12.04 auto); the second had no difference at all (12.01 against 12.04). The effect is inside the run-to-run spread. Setting the vendor hold (power_dpm_force_performance_level=manual + top pp_dpm_fclk) is not a safety fix and not a reliable bandwidth fix; it is a preference.

Caveats worth keeping: the GPU load was weight-streaming pp512, not a decode loop or a render; each cell is a couple of minutes of NPU time, not a soak; and this is one kernel/firmware pair. A long concurrent run with a real provider is still the last unmeasured thing on this route -- but nothing in the fleet needs to serialise NPU behind GPU while waiting for it.
